displayQuote: Please, sir, I want some more

meta.title: Who really said "Please, sir, I want some more"? | Quotle.info
meta.description: Yes, Dickens wrote it. Oliver says it twice in Oliver Twist chapter 2, first printed February 1837. The popular “can I have some more?” is a softening.
meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'Please, sir, I want some more'?
meta.ogDescription: Verified in Oliver Twist ch. 2 — Bentley's Miscellany, Feb 1837, and the 1838 first edition. Oliver says it twice. The “can I have some more?” version is later.

answer.label: Written by
answer.sourceLine: Dickens wrote the line for chapter 2 of Oliver Twist; or, The Parish Boy’s Progress, where the starving nine-year-old says it to the workhouse master — and then, prompted, says it a second time. It reads exactly this way in the very first printing, the February 1837 number of Bentley’s Miscellany, and again in the 1838 first book edition (vol. I, p. 29).

source.excerpt: He rose from the table; and advancing to the master, basin and spoon in hand, said: somewhat alarmed at his own temerity: “Please, sir, I want some more.” The master was a fat, healthy man; but he turned very pale. He gazed in stupefied astonishment on the small rebel for some seconds, and then clung for support to the copper. The assistants were paralysed with wonder; the boys with fear. “What!” said the master at length, in a faint voice. “Please, sir,” replied Oliver, “I want some more.”
trail: First printing. Chapters I and II of Oliver Twist open the February 1837 number of Bentley’s Miscellany, and the line already reads “Please, sir, I want some more.” there — twice — in the scanned volume 1 at the Internet Archive ↗.
First book edition. The three-volume Richard Bentley edition of 1838, published under the pseudonym “Boz,” carries the same sentence on vol. I, p. 29 ↗.

Publication history. Wikipedia records that the novel “was first published in monthly instalments, from February 1837 to April 1839, in the magazine Bentley’s Miscellany ↗,” with the book form issued in three volumes by Richard Bentley.
Reference check. Wikiquote’s sourced entry lists the line under Chapter 2, “Treats Of Oliver Twist’s Growth, Education, And Board” ↗, spoken by Oliver Twist.
source.excerptNote: Quoted from the modern text at Project Gutenberg ↗. The 1838 first edition reads “advancing, basin and spoon in hand, to the master” — the narration around it was lightly reworded in later editions, but Oliver’s two sentences are identical in both.

author.name: Charles Dickens
author.heading: Who wrote it
author.bio: Charles Dickens (7 February 1812 – 9 June 1870) was, in Wikipedia’s phrase, an English writer and journalist — and the defining popular novelist of the Victorian age. Oliver Twist was his second novel, begun while The Pickwick Papers was still running, and he published it under the pen name “Boz.” Wikipedia calls it “the first Victorian novel with a child protagonist” — and Dickens used that child to put the workhouse system on trial in front of readers who had met it only in official reports.

misattribution.heading: What people get wrong
misattribution.intro: The attribution here is solid — the problem is the wording. This is one of the most-quoted sentences in English fiction and one of the most reliably mangled.

items.who: “Please sir, can I have some more?”
items.why: Oliver never asks a question. He states a want: “Please, sir, I want some more.” The polite request is the form the line takes in the 1968 musical film — Wikiquote’s page for Oliver! ↗ transcribes it as “Please sir, can I have some more?” The change is tiny and it costs the scene everything: a demand becomes a request.

items.who: Charles Dickens, quoted as if speaking in his own voice
items.why: Dickens wrote the sentence, but it is dialogue, not authorial statement. It is spoken by a starving workhouse boy who had drawn lots with the others for the job, in chapter 2 of the novel ↗.

He says it twice. The master’s stunned “What!” forces a repetition — “Please, sir,” replied Oliver, “I want some more.” — and it is after the second one that the ladle comes down, as printed in the 1838 first edition, vol. I, p. 29 ↗.

misattribution.truthLine: Dickens wrote it; Oliver speaks it, twice, in chapter 2 — and it has read “I want some more” since its first appearance in February 1837 ↗.

context.heading: Why it mattered
lead: The scene is a set-up. Dickens spends the pages before it explaining, in mock-admiration, how the parish board decided the workhouse poor were having far too pleasant a time and put them on “three meals of thin gruel a-day.” The boys polish their bowls with their spoons until they shine; one of them, tall for his age, hints darkly that unless he gets a second basin he may some night eat the boy sleeping next to him. They cast lots for who will walk up and ask. It falls to Oliver.

So by the time the sentence arrives it is not really a request for food. It is a nine-year-old testing whether the system will admit what it is doing to him — and the answer comes back instantly: a blow from the ladle, instant confinement, and a bill pasted on the gate offering five pounds to anyone who will take Oliver Twist off the parish’s hands.
context.detailsSummary: What happens in the next two pages
detailsBody: Mr. Bumble bursts in on the board “sitting in solemn conclave” to report the offence. Mr. Limbkins asks him to compose himself and confirm that the boy asked for more after eating the supper allotted by the dietary. He did, sir.
The gentleman in the white waistcoat then delivers the verdict the rest of the novel exists to disprove: “That boy will be hung. I know that boy will be hung.” Nobody in the room contradicts him.
Chapter 3 opens by calling the whole episode “the impious and profane offence of asking for more” — the joke the rest of the workhouse satire is built on.
context.pull: Oliver Twist has asked for more!

sourcesVerified.claim: The modern text of Oliver Twist chapter 2 contains “Please, sir, I want some more.” twice, plus the surrounding narration quoted in the excerpt (“He rose from the table; and advancing to the master, basin and spoon in hand…”, the master turning pale, “What!”, the ladle blow, Bumble and Mr. Limbkins, “That boy will be hung.”, the five-pound reward). Chapter II is headed “TREATS OF OLIVER TWIST’S GROWTH, EDUCATION, AND BOARD”, and chapter III opens with “the impious and profane offence of asking for more”.
Project Gutenberg lists the ebook as Oliver Twist by Charles Dickens (1812-1870) with copyright status “Public domain in the USA.”

The 1838 Richard Bentley first edition, vol. I (title page: “OLIVER TWIST; OR, THE PARISH BOY'S PROGRESS. BY ‘BOZ.’ IN THREE VOLUMES. VOL. I. LONDON: RICHARD BENTLEY, NEW BURLINGTON STREET. 1838.”) prints “Please, sir, I want some more.” on page 29, followed by the second occurrence and the ladle blow; its narration reads “advancing basin and spoon in hand, to the master”. Verified against this item's full-text OCR.

Bentley's Miscellany vol. 1 (1837) contains the February 1837 number, whose contents begin at p. 105 (running item “OUR SONG OF THE MONTH. No. II. February, 1837.”; volume index: “Oliver Twist, his birth, 105”), immediately followed by Oliver Twist “CHAPTER THE FIRST” and “CHAPTER THE SECOND”, with “Please, sir, I want some more.” appearing twice inside that installment. Verified against this item's full-text OCR.
Wikiquote's Oliver Twist page lists the sourced entry “Please, sir, I want some more.” attributed to Chapter 2, “Treats Of Oliver Twist's Growth, Education, And Board”, said by Oliver Twist.
Wikiquote's page for the 1968 film Oliver! transcribes Oliver's gruel line as “Please sir, can I have some more?”

Wikipedia states Oliver Twist “was first published in monthly instalments, from February 1837 to April 1839, in the magazine Bentley's Miscellany,” and that it “first appeared in book form … in three volumes published by Richard Bentley, the owner of Bentley's Miscellany, under the author's pseudonym, ‘Boz’.”

Wikipedia gives Charles Dickens's dates as 7 February 1812 – 9 June 1870, describes him as “an English writer and journalist”, and says Oliver Twist “became one of Dickens's better known stories and was the first Victorian novel with a child protagonist.”
Checked whether the Charles Dickens Wikiquote page carries this line — it does not appear there, which is why the Oliver Twist work page was used as the Wikiquote anchor instead.
